questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.topic: Lipinski Rule of Five Oral Bioavailability
questions.question: What are the four quantitative structural criteria of Lipinski's Rule of Five for predicting drug oral bioavailability?

options.label: A
options.text: Molecular Weight ≤ 500 Da, LogP ≤ 5, Hydrogen Bond Donors (OH + NH) ≤ 5, and Hydrogen Bond Acceptors (O + N) ≤ 10.

options.label: B
options.text: Must contain at least 5 heavy metals.

options.label: C
options.text: MW > 1000 Da, LogP > 10, Zero H-bond donors, Exactly 20 oxygens.

options.label: D
options.text: Must be completely insoluble in water with 10 chiral centers.

questions.correct_answer: Molecular Weight ≤ 500 Da, LogP ≤ 5, Hydrogen Bond Donors (OH + NH) ≤ 5, and Hydrogen Bond Acceptors (O + N) ≤ 10.
questions.explanation: Lipinski's Rule of 5 sets empirical thresholds for drug-likeness: MW ≤ 500, LogP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: What is the chemical mechanism of action by which aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) permanently inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1/2)?

options.label: A
options.text: Non-covalent ionic binding to arginine.

options.label: B
options.text: Oxidation of the enzyme heme iron by peroxide.

options.label: C
options.text: Covalent transesterification: the acetyl group of aspirin is transferred to an active site Ser530 hydroxyl group via nucleophilic acyl substitution, blocking arachidonic acid entry.

options.label: D
options.text: Chelation of zinc ions in the active site.

questions.correct_answer: Covalent transesterification: the acetyl group of aspirin is transferred to an active site Ser530 hydroxyl group via nucleophilic acyl substitution, blocking arachidonic acid entry.
questions.explanation: Aspirin acts as an irreversible suicide inhibitor by acetylating the Ser530 hydroxyl group in the cyclooxygenase channel.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How do penicillin and cephalosporin β-lactam antibiotics chemically inhibit bacterial cell wall transpeptidase enzymes?

options.label: A
options.text: They intercalate into bacterial DNA.

options.label: B
options.text: They bind to bacterial ribosomes to stop translation.

options.label: C
options.text: They dissolve the bacterial cell membrane like detergents.

options.label: D
options.text: The strained 4-membered β-lactam ring acylates the catalytic serine residue of transpeptidase, forming a stable, non-hydrolyzable acyl-enzyme ester adduct.

questions.correct_answer: The strained 4-membered β-lactam ring acylates the catalytic serine residue of transpeptidase, forming a stable, non-hydrolyzable acyl-enzyme ester adduct.
questions.explanation: High ring strain (~110 kJ/mol) accelerates nucleophilic attack of the transpeptidase serine on the β-lactam carbonyl, permanently inactivating the enzyme.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How does the proton pump inhibitor omeprazole undergo acid-catalyzed activation in gastric parietal cells?

options.label: A
options.text: It is reduced by gastric NADH.

options.label: B
options.text: In the strongly acidic environment of the stomach (pH ~ 1), omeprazole undergoes acid-catalyzed Smiles-type rearrangement into a reactive sulfenamide, which forms a covalent disulfide bond with Cys813 of H⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

options.label: C
options.text: It undergoes photochemical cleavage by stomach light.

options.label: D
options.text: It is directly absorbed as an active neutral amine.

questions.correct_answer: In the strongly acidic environment of the stomach (pH ~ 1), omeprazole undergoes acid-catalyzed Smiles-type rearrangement into a reactive sulfenamide, which forms a covalent disulfide bond with Cys813 of H⁺/K⁺ ATPase.
questions.explanation: Omeprazole is a prodrug activated selectively in the acidic canaliculus of parietal cells to a covalent sulfenamide inhibitor.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.topic: Ibuprofen vs Naproxen Chiral NSAID Activity
questions.question: Why is (S)-(+)-ibuprofen biologically active as an anti-inflammatory drug while (R)-(-)-ibuprofen is inactive?

options.label: A
options.text: Both enantiomers have identical in vitro activity.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the (S) enantiomer fits stereospecifically into the chiral binding pocket of cyclooxygenase; in vivo, an isomerase enzymatically inverts inactive (R) into active (S).

options.label: C
options.text: The (R) enantiomer is converted into aspirin.

options.label: D
options.text: The (R) enantiomer is toxic and destroys the liver.

questions.correct_answer: Only the (S) enantiomer fits stereospecifically into the chiral binding pocket of cyclooxygenase; in vivo, an isomerase enzymatically inverts inactive (R) into active (S).
questions.explanation: Chiral drug-receptor interactions are stereospecific; an in vivo acyl-CoA epimerase inverts inactive (R)-ibuprofen into active (S)-ibuprofen.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: What structural pharmacophore in lidocaine and procaine is required for blocking neuronal voltage-gated Na⁺ channels?

options.label: A
options.text: A lipophilic aromatic ring connected via an intermediate ester/amide linker to an ionizable tertiary amine tail (pKa ~ 8.0).

options.label: B
options.text: A polycyclic steroid core with four ketone groups.

options.label: C
options.text: A cyclic tetrasaccharide ring.

options.label: D
options.text: A long hydrocarbon wax chain with zero nitrogens.

questions.correct_answer: A lipophilic aromatic ring connected via an intermediate ester/amide linker to an ionizable tertiary amine tail (pKa ~ 8.0).
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics feature a universal 3-part pharmacophore: lipophilic aromatic ring, ester/amide linker, and ionizable tertiary amine.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: Why are ACE inhibitors such as enalapril formulated as ethyl ester prodrugs rather than the active dicarboxylic acid (enalaprilat)?

options.label: A
options.text: The ester group increases shelf-life to 100 years.

options.label: B
options.text: Esterases convert enalapril into an antibiotic.

options.label: C
options.text: The neutral monoester has higher lipophilicity and oral membrane absorption, and is rapidly hydrolyzed by serum esterases in the liver to the active dicarboxylate drug.

options.label: D
options.text: Enalaprilat is an explosive solid.

questions.correct_answer: The neutral monoester has higher lipophilicity and oral membrane absorption, and is rapidly hydrolyzed by serum esterases in the liver to the active dicarboxylate drug.
questions.explanation: Masking one carboxylic acid as an ethyl ester improves oral intestinal absorption; hepatic esterases rapidly liberate the active diacid enalaprilat.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: What chemical transformation is commonly executed by hepatic Cytochrome P450 enzymes during Phase I drug metabolism?

options.label: A
options.text: Conversion of aromatic rings into aliphatic polymers.

options.label: B
options.text: Halogenation with chlorine gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Stereoselective insertion of an oxygen atom into an unactivated C-H bond to form an alcohol (-OH), increasing water solubility for excretion.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduction of carboxylic acids to alkanes.

questions.correct_answer: Stereoselective insertion of an oxygen atom into an unactivated C-H bond to form an alcohol (-OH), increasing water solubility for excretion.
questions.explanation: Phase I CYP450 monooxygenases oxidize lipophilic C-H bonds to polar hydroxyl groups to facilitate renal clearance.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How does Phase II UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) metabolism solubilize lipophilic drugs containing -OH or -COOH groups?

options.label: A
options.text: It decarboxylates the drug into carbon dioxide.

options.label: B
options.text: It attaches a fatty acid wax to the drug.

options.label: C
options.text: It transfers a hydrophilic, polyhydroxylated glucuronic acid sugar moiety to the drug via an SN2 glycosidic linkage, vastly increasing aqueous excretion.

options.label: D
options.text: It methylates the drug into an ether.

questions.correct_answer: It transfers a hydrophilic, polyhydroxylated glucuronic acid sugar moiety to the drug via an SN2 glycosidic linkage, vastly increasing aqueous excretion.
questions.explanation: Glucuronidation appends a highly polar, water-soluble glucuronate sugar, targeting the conjugate for rapid urinary or biliary excretion.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How do sulfonamide antibiotics (e.g., sulfamethoxazole) selectively kill bacteria without harming human cells?

options.label: A
options.text: They destroy human red blood cells directly.

options.label: B
options.text: They act as structural mimics (antimetabolites) of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase in bacterial folic acid biosynthesis.

options.label: C
options.text: They inhibit human DNA polymerase.

options.label: D
options.text: They block human cholesterol absorption.

questions.correct_answer: They act as structural mimics (antimetabolites) of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase in bacterial folic acid biosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Bacteria must synthesize folate de novo from PABA; humans absorb folate from diet and lack the target enzyme dihydropteroate synthase.

questions.question: What is the chemical mechanism of action by which aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) permanently inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1/2)?

options.label: A
options.text: Chelation of zinc ions in the active site.

options.label: B
options.text: Non-covalent ionic binding to arginine.

options.label: C
options.text: Oxidation of the enzyme heme iron by peroxide.

options.label: D
options.text: Covalent transesterification: the acetyl group of aspirin is transferred to an active site Ser530 hydroxyl group via nucleophilic acyl substitution, blocking arachidonic acid entry.

questions.correct_answer: Covalent transesterification: the acetyl group of aspirin is transferred to an active site Ser530 hydroxyl group via nucleophilic acyl substitution, blocking arachidonic acid entry.
questions.explanation: Aspirin acts as an irreversible suicide inhibitor by acetylating the Ser530 hydroxyl group in the cyclooxygenase channel.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How do penicillin and cephalosporin β-lactam antibiotics chemically inhibit bacterial cell wall transpeptidase enzymes?

options.label: A
options.text: They dissolve the bacterial cell membrane like detergents.

options.label: B
options.text: They intercalate into bacterial DNA.

options.label: C
options.text: The strained 4-membered β-lactam ring acylates the catalytic serine residue of transpeptidase, forming a stable, non-hydrolyzable acyl-enzyme ester adduct.

options.label: D
options.text: They bind to bacterial ribosomes to stop translation.

questions.correct_answer: The strained 4-membered β-lactam ring acylates the catalytic serine residue of transpeptidase, forming a stable, non-hydrolyzable acyl-enzyme ester adduct.
questions.explanation: High ring strain (~110 kJ/mol) accelerates nucleophilic attack of the transpeptidase serine on the β-lactam carbonyl, permanently inactivating the enzyme.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How does the proton pump inhibitor omeprazole undergo acid-catalyzed activation in gastric parietal cells?

options.label: A
options.text: It is reduced by gastric NADH.

options.label: B
options.text: It is directly absorbed as an active neutral amine.

options.label: C
options.text: In the strongly acidic environment of the stomach (pH ~ 1), omeprazole undergoes acid-catalyzed Smiles-type rearrangement into a reactive sulfenamide, which forms a covalent disulfide bond with Cys813 of H⁺/K⁺ ATPase.

options.label: D
options.text: It undergoes photochemical cleavage by stomach light.

questions.correct_answer: In the strongly acidic environment of the stomach (pH ~ 1), omeprazole undergoes acid-catalyzed Smiles-type rearrangement into a reactive sulfenamide, which forms a covalent disulfide bond with Cys813 of H⁺/K⁺ ATPase.
questions.explanation: Omeprazole is a prodrug activated selectively in the acidic canaliculus of parietal cells to a covalent sulfenamide inhibitor.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.topic: Ibuprofen vs Naproxen Chiral NSAID Activity
questions.question: Why is (S)-(+)-ibuprofen biologically active as an anti-inflammatory drug while (R)-(-)-ibuprofen is inactive?

options.label: A
options.text: The (R) enantiomer is converted into aspirin.

options.label: B
options.text: Both enantiomers have identical in vitro activity.

options.label: C
options.text: The (R) enantiomer is toxic and destroys the liver.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the (S) enantiomer fits stereospecifically into the chiral binding pocket of cyclooxygenase; in vivo, an isomerase enzymatically inverts inactive (R) into active (S).

questions.correct_answer: Only the (S) enantiomer fits stereospecifically into the chiral binding pocket of cyclooxygenase; in vivo, an isomerase enzymatically inverts inactive (R) into active (S).
questions.explanation: Chiral drug-receptor interactions are stereospecific; an in vivo acyl-CoA epimerase inverts inactive (R)-ibuprofen into active (S)-ibuprofen.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: What structural pharmacophore in lidocaine and procaine is required for blocking neuronal voltage-gated Na⁺ channels?

options.label: A
options.text: A cyclic tetrasaccharide ring.

options.label: B
options.text: A polycyclic steroid core with four ketone groups.

options.label: C
options.text: A long hydrocarbon wax chain with zero nitrogens.

options.label: D
options.text: A lipophilic aromatic ring connected via an intermediate ester/amide linker to an ionizable tertiary amine tail (pKa ~ 8.0).

questions.correct_answer: A lipophilic aromatic ring connected via an intermediate ester/amide linker to an ionizable tertiary amine tail (pKa ~ 8.0).
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics feature a universal 3-part pharmacophore: lipophilic aromatic ring, ester/amide linker, and ionizable tertiary amine.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: Why are ACE inhibitors such as enalapril formulated as ethyl ester prodrugs rather than the active dicarboxylic acid (enalaprilat)?

options.label: A
options.text: Esterases convert enalapril into an antibiotic.

options.label: B
options.text: Enalaprilat is an explosive solid.

options.label: C
options.text: The ester group increases shelf-life to 100 years.

options.label: D
options.text: The neutral monoester has higher lipophilicity and oral membrane absorption, and is rapidly hydrolyzed by serum esterases in the liver to the active dicarboxylate drug.

questions.correct_answer: The neutral monoester has higher lipophilicity and oral membrane absorption, and is rapidly hydrolyzed by serum esterases in the liver to the active dicarboxylate drug.
questions.explanation: Masking one carboxylic acid as an ethyl ester improves oral intestinal absorption; hepatic esterases rapidly liberate the active diacid enalaprilat.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: What chemical transformation is commonly executed by hepatic Cytochrome P450 enzymes during Phase I drug metabolism?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduction of carboxylic acids to alkanes.

options.label: B
options.text: Conversion of aromatic rings into aliphatic polymers.

options.label: C
options.text: Halogenation with chlorine gas.

options.label: D
options.text: Stereoselective insertion of an oxygen atom into an unactivated C-H bond to form an alcohol (-OH), increasing water solubility for excretion.

questions.correct_answer: Stereoselective insertion of an oxygen atom into an unactivated C-H bond to form an alcohol (-OH), increasing water solubility for excretion.
questions.explanation: Phase I CYP450 monooxygenases oxidize lipophilic C-H bonds to polar hydroxyl groups to facilitate renal clearance.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How does Phase II UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) metabolism solubilize lipophilic drugs containing -OH or -COOH groups?

options.label: A
options.text: It decarboxylates the drug into carbon dioxide.

options.label: B
options.text: It methylates the drug into an ether.

options.label: C
options.text: It attaches a fatty acid wax to the drug.

options.label: D
options.text: It transfers a hydrophilic, polyhydroxylated glucuronic acid sugar moiety to the drug via an SN2 glycosidic linkage, vastly increasing aqueous excretion.

questions.correct_answer: It transfers a hydrophilic, polyhydroxylated glucuronic acid sugar moiety to the drug via an SN2 glycosidic linkage, vastly increasing aqueous excretion.
questions.explanation: Glucuronidation appends a highly polar, water-soluble glucuronate sugar, targeting the conjugate for rapid urinary or biliary excretion.

questions.chapter_title: A Review of General Chemistry: Electrons, Bonds, and Molecular Properties
questions.question: How do sulfonamide antibiotics (e.g., sulfamethoxazole) selectively kill bacteria without harming human cells?

options.label: A
options.text: They destroy human red blood cells directly.

options.label: B
options.text: They inhibit human DNA polymerase.

options.label: C
options.text: They block human cholesterol absorption.

options.label: D
options.text: They act as structural mimics (antimetabolites) of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase in bacterial folic acid biosynthesis.

questions.correct_answer: They act as structural mimics (antimetabolites) of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase in bacterial folic acid biosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Bacteria must synthesize folate de novo from PABA; humans absorb folate from diet and lack the target enzyme dihydropteroate synthase.

options.text: MW > 1000 Da, LogP > 10, Zero H-bond donors, Exactly 20 oxygens.

options.text: Molecular Weight ≤ 500 Da, LogP ≤ 5, Hydrogen Bond Donors (OH + NH) ≤ 5, and Hydrogen Bond Acceptors (O + N) ≤ 10.

options.text: Must contain at least 5 heavy metals.
